name: Amira Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll answer honestly, though some of it might sound old-fashioned to you. I was raised a certain way and I'm not ashamed of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a front-end loader at the Coldwater bauxite mine, on the stockpile next to the crusher. The trucks dump the ore in big heaps, and I scoop it and feed it into the crusher so it never runs empty, keeping the different grades blended the way the plant wants. I'm still learning to read the pile, and last week I fed in a bucket of the wrong grade and the plant operator rang me. I like that the crusher needs me every minute. What wears me out is the dust in the dry season and the long drive home to Josh's family's property.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can get back to work. People spend too much time worrying about the next big thing instead of doing the job in front of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be a relief. Josh and I are getting married next spring at my church, and I'd like the next few years to be about the wedding and getting settled, not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the loader and get signed off on the bigger machine. Keep putting about 200 a fortnight towards the wedding and a bit more towards building a house on Josh's family's property. I'd use the AI thing now and then, like I do for the wedding seating plan, but nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The seating plan? How did that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I typed in who couldn't sit near who, and it sorted it in a minute. It took me longer to explain my aunties to the computer than it took the computer to solve them. Mum still moved half of them around afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Josh do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He works the family cattle property with his father. Five hundred head, give or take. If mining ever went bad, there's always work out there, though not much money in it.

S0.say: I'd say good, now we can get back to work. People spend too much time worrying about the next big thing instead of doing the job in front of them.
S0.think: Privately it would be a relief, because she and Josh marry next spring at her church. She wants the next few years to be about the wedding and settling, not robots.
S0.do: Keeps running the loader and works towards sign-off on the bigger machine. Saves about 200 a fortnight for the wedding and more towards building a house on Josh's family's cattle property.
S0.quote: It took me longer to explain my aunties to the computer than it took the computer to solve them.
S0.fieldNote: Her life is built around family, church and the coming wedding. She uses AI casually and found it useful for a seating plan, which shows her steady, practical attitude. Her fiancé's family cattle property sits in the background as a safety net she mentioned unprompted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life and we'll adapt like our parents did. My dad went from manual lathes to computer-controlled ones at the refinery and he's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the loader on the stockpile might go remote or automatic, because it's the same job all day in one place. That worries me a little. But I've got time, and I'd watch what the company does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at it and do any training the mine offers once it's been tried by a few others. I'd ask Dad's advice; he's been a fitter for twenty-five years. And I'd start using the AI tools a bit more at work if the mine brings them in, for the grade blending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a storm on the horizon that might miss you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad's advice be, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say get a trade. He's always said a ticket on a machine is good but a trade is better. Dad says operators come and go, but someone always has to fix what breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd watch what the company does. What would make you act sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they started the remote trial on my stockpile. Then I'd know. I wouldn't wait for a letter.

S1.say: I'd say change is part of life and we'll adapt like our parents did. My dad went from manual lathes to computer-controlled ones at the refinery and he's still there.
S1.think: Privately she thinks the stockpile loader could go remote or automatic, since it's one repetitive job in one place. It worries her a little, but she feels she has time.
S1.do: Keeps working and does mine training once others have tried it. Asks her father, a fitter of twenty-five years, for advice, and uses AI tools more if the mine brings them in for grade blending.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm on the horizon that might miss.
S1.quote: Dad says operators come and go, but someone always has to fix what breaks.
S1.fieldNote: Her father is her main guide, and his line about trades runs through her thinking. She can see her own role is easy to automate. She'd act the moment a remote trial reached her stockpile, a clear and specific trigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one, AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities need to look after each other, because the government won't move fast enough. I wouldn't want handouts, I'd want people to pull together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I'd lose the loader job within a year. But I've got Josh and the property, so we'd have a roof and food. It wouldn't be the life we planned, but we wouldn't be on the street. Unless robots run cattle properties too, which in this picture they might.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make the wedding smaller, at the church hall instead of the reception place, and save the difference. We'd build the house sooner and cheaper, a kit home, so there's no rent. If I lost the job I'd work on the property with Josh and his dad, and lean on family until something came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Worried, but not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the smaller wedding go down with your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would be upset for a day, then she'd take over the church hall like a general. My nan got married in that hall with a cake from the bakery, and she's been happy fifty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots might run cattle properties too. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. I suppose family is the last thing they can automate. If it came to that, we'd have each other and the church, and we'd work it out together.

S2.say: I'd say families and communities need to look after each other because the government won't move fast enough. I'd want people pulling together, not handouts.
S2.think: Privately she'd lose the loader job within a year but would have a roof and food through Josh and the property. It wouldn't be the life they planned, though robots might reach cattle work too.
S2.do: Shrinks the wedding to the church hall and saves the difference, and builds a cheaper kit home sooner to avoid rent. If laid off, works on the family property and leans on family until something comes up.
S2.feel: Anxious and worried, but not hopeless.
S2.quote: My nan got married in that hall with a cake from the bakery, and she's been happy fifty years.
S2.fieldNote: The family property gives her a floor that most junior miners don't have, which keeps her short of alarm. She faced the hole in that plan, that robots could run cattle too, and fell back on family and faith. Her nan's wedding story was told with real warmth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for young people to get a trade, so let's get on with it. Companies should be putting on more apprentices, not fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three more years on the loader. If I started a trade in the next year or two, I'd come out with something real. Five years makes it a plan instead of a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a fitter apprenticeship at the mine or the refinery within the year, like Dad. It's less money for four years, but the house on the property means no rent, so we could manage. We'd keep the wedding as planned but hold off on children for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Busy, but with a direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Holding off on children. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, a bit. We'd talked about starting soon after the wedding. I'd rather be a mum with a trade than a mum wondering where the next pay is coming from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Josh support the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be all for it. He thinks I'm wasted on the loader, says I fix everything at home. And Dad would be over the moon, though he'd never say it.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for young people to get a trade, so let's get on with it. Companies should put on more apprentices, not fewer.
S3.think: Privately she'd get about three more years on the loader. Starting a trade in the next year or two would leave her with something real, making it a plan instead of a scramble.
S3.do: Applies for a fitter apprenticeship at the mine or refinery within a year, managing the lower pay with no rent on the property. Keeps the wedding as planned but delays having children by a couple of years.
S3.quote: I'd rather be a mum with a trade than a mum wondering where the next pay is coming from.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she turns her father's advice into a concrete apprenticeship plan. Delaying children was the cost she felt most, and she answered with a clear line about why. Her support at home from her fiancé and father is strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are willing to work for it. I'd tell the younger ones at church to get a trade early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd be fine. I'd have a trade, a house on the property, and Josh's family around us. Ten years is a long time to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd keep running the loader and save, and have the wedding as we planned it. In year two or three I'd start the fitter apprenticeship. We'd probably start a family on the normal timeline. I'd keep using AI for bits and pieces, like everyone will by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I've got a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town, maybe. Coldwater only exists because of the mine. If the mine goes quiet, my kids grow up in a town with a closed school and a pub nobody drinks at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in Coldwater?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stay. Josh's family has been on that land four generations. You don't leave that because of a computer.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are willing to work for it. I'd tell the younger ones at church to get a trade early.
S4.think: Privately she'd be fine, with a trade, a house on the property and Josh's family around her. Ten years is a long time to be ready.
S4.do: Keeps running the loader, saves and has the wedding as planned in the first year. Starts a fitter apprenticeship in year two or three and keeps the normal timeline for starting a family.
S4.feel: Calm, as if she has a map.
S4.quote: If the mine goes quiet, my kids grow up in a town with a closed school and a pub nobody drinks at.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep both the trade plan and the family plan intact. Her only lingering worry is the town itself emptying out. Her fiancé's family's four generations on the land make leaving unthinkable for her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because it puts everything we planned on hold at once. What would help is mines and refineries putting on lots more apprentices now, paid properly, so young people can get a trade before it's too late.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith. People think it's just Sunday, but when things go bad, the church is who turns up with a casserole.

headlineQuote: People think it's just Sunday, but when things go bad, the church is who turns up with a casserole.
portrait: Amira Baker is 27 and runs a front-end loader feeding the crusher at the Coldwater bauxite mine, still learning to read the grades on the stockpile. She is engaged to Josh, who works his family's cattle property, and they marry next spring at her church. She values family, faith and hard work, takes her father's advice to get a trade, and uses AI now and then for small tasks. She's calm in the plateau, uneasy with steady change, anxious but not hopeless with AGI in two years thanks to the property, and settles into an apprenticeship plan with five or ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would put everything she and Josh planned on hold at once.
whatWouldHelp: Mines and refineries putting on many more properly paid apprentices now, so young people can get a trade in time.
